w: Phase I is the non-surgical stage every periodontal patient starts with, whatever the stage. These notes combine the 2026 slide deck with the recorded class session. Dr. Kaur framed D2 as a step past D1: less about fundamentals, more about therapy, when it succeeds and fails, and what options exist, all to get you ready for clinic next year. She spent the session on the exam and the reasoning behind therapy, and deliberately left instrument detail for the upcoming PCD sessions. Midterm scope (Dr. Kaur's email after class): you will not be tested on instruments, ultrasonics or polishing. Focus on the class discussion and the slides up to failure of therapy. In these notes, that means everything down to the section on Phase I evaluation and failure. The sections after it are marked. Flagged in class: the host-bacteria pathogenesis diagram (health → gingivitis → periodontitis) was introduced with "how many times you have seen this before, has anybody been counting? That's going to be on the quiz." Know who initiates the disease, who drives it, and what SRP actually targets. Start from the diagnosis Every patient in the chair lands in one of three broad categories: health, gingivitis or periodontitis. Health and gingivitis can each sit on an intact or a reduced periodontium. Periodontitis cannot sit on an intact periodontium, because underlying bone loss is what separates it from the other two. You can't tell the three apart just by looking, whether from a photo or the patient's mouth. Tissue appearance is only one piece. An accurate diagnosis needs the full charting (probing depth, recession, attachment loss, furcations, mobility, tissue health) combined with the radiographs. The exam: plaque and gingival health A complete periodontal exam covers oral hygiene (plaque index), gingival health, probing, attachment level, furcations, the mucogingival complex, mobility, occlusion and radiographs. It always starts with oral hygiene, because plaque is the primary etiologic factor. There are two ways to capture plaque. You can run the probe about 1 mm into the sulcus or pocket (not the same as measuring probing depth) and score each site 1 if you pick up plaque and 0 if you don't. Or the patient chews a disclosing tablet (lavender or pink, in the clinic inventory), rinses briefly, and you clear excess solution off the cheeks and tongue, show them in a mirror and record the index. Both methods record only presence or absence, not quantity. Quantifying plaque (gingival third, half the tooth, the whole tooth) at every site would take far more chair time. Gingival health is read from color (erythema), texture (edema), bleeding on probing and a gingival index. BOP is captured while you probe: a site that bleeds scores 1, one that doesn't scores 0. Delayed bleeding counts. When you've moved on to the next quadrant or the next two teeth, look back. Sites that have started bleeding since are still scored 1. Not every periodontitis case looks the same, because risk factors change the clinical picture. Smoking masks inflammation: nicotine's vasoconstriction tends to leave the tissue looking cyanotic rather than edematous and hemorrhagic. Diabetes exaggerates it. Drug-induced gingival overgrowth is a sign that something in the medical or social history is adding to the picture. The class example was a hypertensive patient on amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker, with bulbous enlargement mostly in the interdental tissue, and more on the buccal/labial than the lingual/palatal. The four patients shown (all from the student clinic) all had periodontitis. One was stage 1, one stage 2, and one had stage 2 with uncontrolled diabetes plus a calcium channel blocker, yet each looked different. Probing, recession and CAL Probing records six sites per tooth (DB, B, MB, DL, L, ML), taking the deepest reading on each. Probing depth runs from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. Recession runs from the CEJ to the gingival margin. Clinical attachment level runs from the CEJ to the base of the pocket, so CAL = PD + GR. The deck's paired examples: a 7 mm pocket with no recession and a 2 mm pocket with 5 mm of recession both have a CAL of 7 mm. The lecture's main point about these numbers: in health, probing depth is not equal to clinical attachment level. In intact tissue the gingival margin sits slightly coronal to the CEJ and hides it. Recession is positive when there is true recession (you can see the CEJ) and negative when the margin is coronal to the CEJ: −1, −2, −3, or −3 to −4 or more with drug-induced overgrowth. Add it with its sign. PD 5 mm with GR −3 mm gives CAL 2 mm. Skip the recession and that same site reads CAL 5 mm, which would push you toward Stage 3 or 4 even though the radiographs may show only about 20% bone loss. Probing depth, CAL and the radiographs have to tell the same story. The same trap is built into Salud. Leave recession blank, or type 0 without checking whether it is really positive or negative, and Salud sets CAL equal to PD. A blank over-diagnoses disease, and a reflexive zero gives an inaccurate diagnosis too. Only when you enter the signed value does Salud calculate CAL correctly. To measure negative recession, you have to feel the CEJ, because you can't see it. Walk the probe to the base of the pocket, then slowly draw it out until you feel the rough CEJ. The millimeters still under the margin at that point are the negative GR, which you subtract from PD. It's harder with heavy inflammation or gingival overgrowth (both pathologic), with altered passive eruption (physiologic), and with calculus or restorative margins that can feel like a CEJ. Some background on eruption: as a tooth comes in, active eruption moves the tooth toward occlusion, while passive eruption is the gingiva, with its connective tissue and junctional epithelium, migrating apically to settle at the CEJ. In altered passive eruption the tissue never makes that move, so the margin ends up well coronal to the CEJ. Expect a learning curve here. The probe is the most important instrument in the exam. Use light pressure, feel for the elastic stop, and keep it parallel to the long axis. Interproximal probing is not line-angle probing. Stopping at the line angle is wrong. Carry the probe past the line angle and under the contact point (anteriors) or contact area (posteriors), tilted slightly toward the area apical to the contact. The usual errors are too little angulation or too much. When you can't probe yet: debridement Debridement is not a therapeutic procedure. You never do it to treat disease, and it should never be combined with scaling and root planing. Its only indication is that calculus hides the gingival margin so completely that you can't see or explore it, and so can't capture any numbers. There is only a full-mouth debridement code. No half-mouth, lower-anterior or maxillary-posterior version exists. The code is intended for generalized calculus heavy enough to cover even chewing surfaces, and you will seldom see that. Insurance won't pay for debridement and a periodontal exam at the same visit, on the reasoning that if you couldn't probe before, the tissue won't be ready right after. So in practice the patient comes back in about two weeks for full charting. At school it's more flexible. First-time perio charting is free, so after debriding a localized bridge of calculus you can go straight on to full-mouth charting in the same visit if the tissue holds up. Check with your faculty, who may prefer to let it settle for two weeks. Combining the two saves the patient a visit. In private practice you can choose not to bill the debridement at all, though a fully booked hygiene schedule is often a reason to stagger the appointments anyway. Furcations: Glickman, not millimeters Furcations are examined with the Nabers probe. It is curved, with alternating light and dark bands 3 mm apart, and it is read alongside radiographs. Even though it has markings, the language used here is the Glickman classification, not a millimeter scale. Class I is not "3 mm or less." Class I, incipient. The probe just feels a catch. Usually needs no treatment, and it is easy to maintain as long as attachment loss and probing depth don't increase. Class II, cul-de-sac. A definite furcation invasion, but a bony wall remains on the other side (probe from buccal and the palatal or lingual crest is still there). It has depth and containability, so it is the class most amenable to regeneration. Class III, through-and-through. The hardest to treat. With no containability left, it has lost its regenerative potential. Class IV. A class III that has also lost the soft tissue over it, naturally through recession or surgically, so the through-and-through furcation is visible. The patient can clean it with interdental aids or a water flosser, but the exposed root trunk risks sensitivity and root caries. Caries in a furcation makes the tooth hopeless, so keep these teeth under close watch at every maintenance visit. Dr. Kaur's cases: an upper molar (#3) with distopalatal and straight buccal involvement was the only distal abutment of a bridge, so rather than extract it, the class III was converted to class IV (furcation cleaned, margin moved apically for access). That patient is still doing well. Another patient with the same treatment developed a large carious lesion under the furcation roof. Mucogingival exam, mobility and occlusion The mucogingival exam asks how much keratinized tissue the patient has. Measure its width directly, or use the rolling technique: roll the mucosa coronally until you reach the mucogingival junction, beyond which it won't roll. This matters around implants as well as teeth. Recession and overgrowth are noted here too. Mobility is checked with two rigid (blunt) instruments, one on each side of the tooth, and graded on the Miller scale: 0 is normal, 1 is slightly more than normal (<1 mm), 2 is moderately more (>1 mm but <2 mm), and 3 is severe faciolingual and/or mesiodistal mobility combined with vertical displacement. A tooth that is depressible in its socket is ready for extraction. That's static mobility. Fremitus is mobility in function. You rest a finger on the root while the patient brings the teeth together and feel for vibration. It can have a vertical and/or horizontal component, and it is palpated, not seen, unless it is extreme. Positive fremitus means you need to find out why the tooth carries that load. In the class example, lack of posterior support meant the premolars were doing the work of molars. The perio chart has no place for occlusal findings, so record them in the notes section: wear patterns, erosion, vertical defects and whether they tie to an occlusal problem, and parafunctional habits. That matters because mobility isn't always from periodontitis alone. It can be occlusal trauma on a reduced periodontium, from lack of posterior support, parafunction, or overjet and overbite. Treating a 5 mm pocket won't resolve grade 2 mobility unless the occlusion is addressed. The deck's list of occlusal signs: parafunctional habits, mobility, fremitus, migration, open contacts, atypical wear and wear facets, possible TMJ pain, infrabony defects and a widened PDL space. Radiographs, before you touch the patient Before any clinical data, a radiograph can show you whether there is bone loss, where it is (localized or generalized) and its pattern (horizontal, vertical, or both). It also shows tipped teeth, fused roots, root proximity (important for surgical and non-surgical therapy), calculus, sinus proximity, and a periapical lesion (#7 in the class film). Seeing calculus on a radiograph should make you "a little bit of both" sad and excited. Sad the patient got there, excited because you now know the cause and it is something you can remove. Once calculus has formed the patient can't remove it, so your role matters even more. Her practical tip: when you sit down for SRP (or even a prophy), don't open the chart to hunt for deep pockets. The instrument will find the pocket, and its base is your limit. Open the x-rays instead (screenshot them, since Salud times out). Then roughness on #14-15 matches calculus you've already seen, and exudate or a sinus tract on #7 matches the PA lesion. Always look at the x-rays before you start capturing numbers. Why Phase I works: bacteria start it, the host drives it Plaque bacteria initiate the disease. The host immune response drives its progression. In health the host is responsive and the bacterial load isn't virulent enough, so inflammation is fought off acutely before disease surfaces. In gingivitis the bacterial composition shifts and the attack gets more aggressive. The host still wins, but it takes longer: T cells and B cells are recruited alongside PMNs, and you see inflammation for days to weeks. Not every patient moves from reversible to irreversible inflammation. Those who do have a host that has become hyper-responsive, whether to the same bacteria or a heavier attack, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines. Environmental, genetic, behavioral and epigenetic factors add risk. The picture of periodontitis is attachment loss, bone loss, loss of PDL, cementum and alveolar bone. SRP targets the bacteria, yet bacteria cause only about 25% of the damage. About 75% comes from the host's inflammatory mediators and bone-destroying cells (osteoclasts). Bacteria bring endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide), not osteoclasts. Removing the bacteria calms the host response. When even good home care plus the best SRP or surgery leaves residual disease, you can also calm the host directly. That is host modulation, or "periodontal medicine," covered later by Dr. Litz. Bacteria cover calculus and live inside its tubules. Calculus and plaque also act as irritants the host reacts to, supra- or subgingivally. The goals of removing them: reduce inflammation, shift the pocket flora from gram-negative toward gram-positive (healthy mouths still have bacteria, just different ones), and arrest progression. SRP does not reverse the damage. Lost bone and attachment stay lost, which is why periodontitis is called irreversible. And pocket elimination is not the rationale for SRP, even though pockets do shrink. A pocket is a space the patient can't clean, filled with more virulent gram-negative flora and facing the host response. Phase I changes that local environment. How pockets shrink, and why re-evaluate at 4-6 weeks Two changes reduce probing depth. At the gingival margin: inflammation means increased volume (cells and fluid, inside and outside cells). As it resolves the tissue shrinks, which you record clinically as increased recession. At the base of the pocket: disease had broken both the junctional epithelium (which is why the probe sank deeper) and the connective tissue fibers. After SRP both reattach to the clean root. The measurement is two-dimensional, but the disease is three-dimensional. The healing clock: junctional epithelium 7-10 days, connective tissue reattachment 4-6 weeks, and collagen fiber maturation and orientation 3-6 months. That is why the patient returns at 4-6 weeks. You see the maximum result by then, and research shows waiting longer gives no additional pocket reduction. The deck puts it slightly differently: the biggest PD changes happen in the first 4 weeks, the dentogingival junction is re-established at 2-4 weeks, and repair and maturation can continue for 9-12 months. Know both sets of numbers. The deck's "6 mm might become 5 or 4.5" figures are there for a sense of scale. She said you are not expected to memorize them. The vocabulary (and the codes) Scaling removes soft and hard deposits from tooth and root surfaces and from any fixed or removable prosthesis, both supra- and subgingivally. If asked whether scaling is supra- or sub-G, the answer is both. Root planing stays subgingival and works only on root surfaces, removing cementum or surface dentin that is rough, calculus-impregnated or contaminated, to leave a smooth root with no ridges, roughness or catch. Clinically the two are done together. Prophylaxis is preventive, not therapeutic. It is for a patient who has never had periodontitis (gingival health or gingivitis). Subgingival calculus doesn't make it periodontitis: normal sulci have depth, and calculus 1-2 mm down is subgingival and gets removed as part of the prophy. Periodontal maintenance is supportive therapy for a patient already treated for periodontitis, to keep the disease from recurring, with oral hygiene evaluated every visit. The terms are not interchangeable. A maintenance patient with mostly 1-3 mm pockets, some residual 4s and an isolated 5 is fine to stay on maintenance when hygiene is good, those sites don't bleed, the tissue looks healthy and the radiographs show no progression. Localized SRP on residual pockets that didn't respond is defined as part of maintenance. Scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346) sits between a prophy and SRP. It is for a patient never diagnosed with periodontitis who has no bone loss but heavy, generalized inflammation from local factors (plaque and calculus), so a simple prophy undersells the work. At school it's done the perio way, with perio faculty or a resident, and gets a Phase I evaluation. The class case was a young patient (20s to early 30s) with a lingual bridge of calculus. What looked like bone loss around the premolars and mesial of the molars came from second premolars extracted for orthodontics and the tipping that followed, not from periodontitis. Diagnosis: generalized gingival inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient (the deck calls it gingivitis on a reduced periodontium), treated with D4346. That case had debridement, charting and therapy in the same visit. Full-mouth debridement (D4355) is gross removal so a proper evaluation can be done at a later visit. What the evidence says about delivery There is no considerable advantage to spreading instrumentation over multiple sessions: calculus left behind after several visits stays for the same reasons it stays after one (Anderson et al. 1996). Manual and mechanically driven (ultrasonic) instrumentation show no statistical difference in probing-depth reduction or attachment gain, and adding subgingival irrigation with chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide adds nothing. Root debridement is inadequate about 65% of the time in pockets ≥5 mm (Greenstein 2000). The limitations, as she taught them: deeper pockets are harder to reach, though a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean calculus is left every time. SRP is a blinded procedure: tactile sensation and proprioception are your guide in the pocket. Motile bacteria invade the pocket lining, while SRP only targets the pocket itself (and it doesn't reliably suppress A. actinomycetemcomitans). Restorations with overhanging, subgingival, open or rough margins both collect plaque and resist cleaning. Furcations and developmental grooves, fissures and concavities block access. Chasing a smooth root can remove too much cementum, causing hypersensitivity. And results depend on the patient's compliance with hygiene and on operator skill, which has a learning curve. Phase I evaluation, and when it "fails" Re-evaluate at 4-6 weeks: plaque scores, signs of inflammation, BOP, PD, recession, CAL, mobility, furcation and suppuration. This is the visit where the decision about surgery is made. If there's still inflammation and the numbers haven't improved, check whether residual calculus is the reason. You'll often feel it with the probe while recharting. If it is, remove it (not charged) and do another Phase I evaluation in two weeks. If you already removed all the deposits the first time, more rounds of SRP won't do anything. What works is improving the patient's oral hygiene. "Failure of therapy" is a harsh term, because so much is outside your control. The host response matters to healing as well as to disease. A smoker or a patient with uncontrolled diabetes may not get the same short- or long-term result from your best SRP. The deck's approach to a failed Phase I: assess the tissue response, remaining deposits, health history and risk factors, possibly a plaque culture. Then choose among antibiotics or antimicrobials, host modulation, repeating non-surgical therapy, another re-evaluation, or Phase II, which is surgical therapy to eliminate pockets. The instruments (not on the midterm) Per Dr. Kaur's email, instruments, ultrasonics and polishing are off the midterm, and in the deck they come after failure of therapy. The email only covers the midterm, so this material can still come back on the comprehensive final and in the PCD instrument competency. She deliberately kept instruments light this session. They get dissected in the upcoming PCD sessions, and you don't need the numbers yet, though you will later. For now, three sets live on your daily kits. The exam kit holds the mirror, the periodontal probe, the Nabers probe for furcations, and a periodontal explorer. That explorer is not the caries explorer. You use it after therapy to check for smooth roots or any catch or roughness. Then come scalers and curettes. Every instrument has a handle, a shank and a blade (the shank connects the two). Scalers are mainly supragingival. They reach only a short way subgingivally (the deck says 1-2 mm; in class she said about 2-3, noting sources give 1-3 or 1-2). Working strokes are short, powerful and fast. Curettes travel deep into the pocket with longer, slightly lighter strokes that take more time, though tenacious calculus can still need real pressure. The key difference is the blade. A scaler has cutting edges on both sides. A Gracey curette cuts on one side only, so subgingivally the side facing the soft tissue is protected. Nearly every curette on the kit is a Gracey, marked SG, site-specific with one cutting edge. The single SC instrument is the one universal curette, which, like a scaler, has a blade on both sides. The clinic has piezoelectric ultrasonic handpieces and tips alongside hand instruments. They can be used subgingivally, but they cannot root plane, so they won't leave a smooth root. Use them in combination: ultrasonic to remove gross deposits, then hand instruments, then the ultrasonic again so the irrigation's lavage flushes the pocket. From the deck, for later: periodontal hand instruments are mirrors, explorers, probes, scaling and root-planing instruments, and polishing instruments. The mirror gives indirect vision, illumination and retraction. The ODU 11/12 explorer is used on every surface of every tooth to feel root roughness. Its shank resembles the Gracey 11/12, and it is inserted with the terminal shank parallel to the tooth down to the slight resistance of the epithelial attachment, using up-and-down and side-to-side strokes with the side of the tip. The UNC-15 probe is 15 mm long. The exam kit is probe, explorer, Nabers probe, mirror and cotton pliers. Sickle scalers have a pointed tip, a triangular cross-section and two cutting edges. Use on exposed cementum is restricted. They work with a short, powerful pull stroke under the ledge of calculus, using the lower third of the blade. The H6/7 anterior sickle has a straight shank for anterior teeth and the buccal/lingual of molars. The S204SD9 posterior sickle has a right-angled shank for posterior interproximals. Both work at about 80° to the root. A curette has a rounded tip and a half-circle cross-section and works supra- and subgingivally. A universal curette (Columbia 13/14) has two cutting edges. An area-specific Gracey has one. Gracey curettes have a 70° blade angle, a single cutting edge on the lower side of the blade, a rounded back that protects the tissue, and a lower shank that should sit parallel to the long axis of the tooth. Each is inserted at a closed angle, then opened to a 70-80° working angle against the root. The 3/4 (or 1/2, 7/8) covers all surfaces of anterior teeth (the demo slide adds premolars) and deep subgingival calculus. The 11/12 covers mesial surfaces of posterior teeth plus the buccal/lingual of molars. The 15/16 is an alternative mesial-posterior instrument. The 13/14 covers distal surfaces of posterior teeth: its shank has more bends than the 11/12, and it is pulled apico-coronally or postero-anteriorly. Ultrasonics come in two types. A magnetostrictive unit sends electrical energy to nickel-iron metal stacks in the insert, which change shape and vibrate in an elliptical-to-orbital pattern at roughly 18,000-42,000 cycles per second, so every surface of the tip can debride. A piezoelectric unit uses crystals in the handpiece, and the tip moves linearly, so mainly its lateral surfaces work. For implants, probes are marked in 3-mm sections (3-6-9-12 or 3-6-8-11), and the listed instruments are anterior and posterior sickles plus the Columbia 4R/4L. Technique (not on the midterm) Don't forget (the deck's own emphasis): modified pen grasp and a finger rest. There are four intraoral finger rests: conventional (tooth surfaces right next to the working area), cross-arch (the other side of the same arch), opposite-arch (the opposite arch), and finger-on-finger (the index finger or thumb of the non-working hand). Adaptation depends on the tissue (fibrotic vs. hemorrhagic), the severity of disease (how retractable the tissue is, the interproximal embrasure), and how tenacious the calculus is. An exploratory stroke uses light force with the instrument adapted, to map the depth and topography of the pocket and find calculus. A working stroke uses a tight grasp with pressure through the working end: scaling strokes are short, overlapping, powerful and controlled, and root-planing strokes are longer and shaving, with lighter pressure. You check your work during the session by exploring the root surface, and at Phase I evaluation by the tissue response: less erythema, edema and BOP. The patient's own hygiene weighs heavily on that result. The areas most often missed are the CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles and hard-to-reach areas, especially distal surfaces of posterior teeth. To polish or not to polish (not on the midterm) For polishing: it removes extrinsic stain that brushing and scaling leave, prepares teeth for sealants, fluoride gels and varnishes, and patients like it. Against: 30 seconds with pumice can remove up to 4 µm of enamel, and the outermost layer holds the most fluoride. A coarse abrasive can leave a rougher surface than it started with. Steady pressure from a fast rubber cup can cause pain and possible pulpal damage. A rubber cup with pumice for 2 minutes can strip the sulcular epithelium entirely, and pumice can be pushed subgingivally. If you polish, use a low-abrasion paste on a slow-speed handpiece with minimal heat, the cup at 90° to the tooth, and intermittent light pressure. (Polishing came from the deck. It wasn't covered in the recorded session.)
